newsitem.title: USA: Skull unveiled of largest predator dinosaur.
newsitem.headline: Skull unveiled of largest predator dinosaur.

text.p: Scientists on Friday unveiled the reconstructed skull of the largest species of meat-eating dinosaur ever found, cementing its reputation as "an absolutely terrifying predatory machine."

The dagger-toothed dinosaur, named Giganotosaurus carolinii, was an estimated 45-47 feet (13.7-14.3 metres) long and weighed 7.7-8.8 tons (7-8 metric tons) when it lived some 97 million years ago, said its discoverer, Argentine paleontologist Rodolpho Coria.
That is about five feet (1.5 metres) longer and two tons (1.8 metric tons) heavier than the previous king of dinosaur predators, Tyrannosaurus Rex.
The first reconstruction of the beast's 6 foot (1.8 metre) long skull was unveiled on Friday at the Academy of Natural Sciences, a pioneering institution of dinosaur research.
The entire reconstructed skeleton will go on display at the academy on June 13.

Discovery of the dinosaur's remarkably complete skeleton near a lake in western Argentina was announced in 1995 by Coria, who is director of the Carmen Fuenes Museum in Plaza Huincul, Argentina. The first bones were unearthed by an amateur paleontologist.
"We are looking at the upper end of the bio-energetically permissible size range for a predator," University of Pennsylvania paleontologist Peter Dobson said at the event.
Running on its two hind legs, the flesh-ripping creature probably chased down and ate plant-eaters at least twice its size.
Its 76 dagger-shapped teeth set in long, narrow jaws made for "collectively, just an absolutely horrifying predatory machine," Dobson said.
In contrast, T. Rex, with heavier teeth and a more-blocky skull suited to crushing bones, most likely scavenged the bodies of dead dinosaurs, the scientists said.

Coria said the Giganotosaurus was remarkably similar to another predator from the same era found in Africa, indicating the continents may have separated about 10 million years later than previous theories have held.
Dobson said recent discoveries also indicated the centre of dinosaur evolution may have been in the southern hemisphere, and not North America as previously thought.
Giganotosaurus was large and ferocious, but it was not very smart, even for a dinosaur. Its brain was about the size of a banana, and less developed than the T. Rex's, Coria said.
"T. Rex was much more bright and much more sophisticated than Giganotosaurus," he said.
And although Giganotosaurus may be pushing 100 million years in age, it is thoroughly modern -- it already has its own web site. Internet surfers can find the dinosaur at www.giganotosaurus.com.
